page.title: Fluency substitution
page.description: Two associates hand in the same AI-drafted patent claims. Changing one fact shows which of them owns the reasoning.
page.setup: Two junior associates at a patent law firm get the same task, the same inventor's notes and the same AI: draft a client's patent claims, the sentences that set what an invention protects. The first has the AI draft them, reads the draft closely and agrees with it. The second first writes down what's new and how it works, then has the AI draft from that. Suppose both hand in the very same claims. The same goes for any polished draft you sign: change one fact, and you find out whether the reasoning in it is yours. This is fluency substitution: polished analysis stands in for owned reasoning. Illustration based on Autor et al. (2026). The associates, the invention and the older patent are constructed.
page.srTitle: Fluency substitution, an animated figure in twelve beats
page.srSummary: An animated figure that opens on its name, Fluency substitution, failure mode 2 of 7, and builds a table. A red dot stands for an associate at a patent law firm with an example task: draft the claims for a client's invention, a wearable that reads heart rate. An AI drafts polished claims, shown in grey on a beige band, the figure's mark for words the AI wrote: claim reading through clothing broadly, since no earlier device does it; as a narrower claim, the sensor's fabric adjustment; as the fallback, the battery design. The associate reads it closely and agrees with every line. A second associate first writes down in a red note what is new and how it works, "it reads heart rate through clothing, by adjusting its sensor to each fabric", then has an AI draft from it. Suppose that draft matches the first one word for word. The partner receives two identical drafts, both tagged as drafted with AI. With the drafts set aside, the partner asks each associate what they would claim and why, and both explain clearly: reading through clothing, which no device has done before. Their answers appear in plain ink, as the partner would hear them. Then one fact changes: an older patent already covers reading through clothing. The first associate takes the draft's fallback: lead with the battery design. The second leads with the sensor that adjusts to each fabric. Then the partner adds that the older patent covers the battery too, so only the sensor is still new. Only then do the answers take their colours, to show whose words they are: the draft's words in the first associate's answers turn the AI's grey, and the associates' own words turn red. The figure ends on the name and its definition, "Polished analysis stands in for owned reasoning.", then the partner’s check and the follow-up, with a source line: illustration based on Autor et al. (2026). Each beat is listed below with what is on screen.

page.checkFollow: Both associates in the figure explain the claims clearly without the draft. The second line separates them. It comes from *The Irreducible Officer*, an essay written for military education, which looks for the person who "revises under challenge rather than retreating to the artifact's language".
evidence: In a pre-registered three-month randomized trial, David Autor and colleagues gave "133 practicing patent lawyers at eleven U.S. intellectual property law firms" access to a custom AI patent drafting assistant. Of those, 91 completed the full protocol. Expert raters, blind to who had the tool, scored the work.

The paper's abstract states the finding: "AI access raised the quality of work delivered on benchmark patent drafting tasks at 10 days (0.34 SD, p = 0.03) and 90 days (0.38 SD, p = 0.01), with larger gains among junior lawyers."

At the end, the 91 lawyers who completed the study each reviewed and corrected an existing patent application without AI. "Treated lawyers outperformed controls by 0.32 SD (p = 0.04), but this advantage was concentrated entirely among senior lawyers (0.45 SD, p = 0.02). Junior lawyers showed no average gain. Their scores instead bifurcated, with sharply fewer mediocre scores offset by more poor and more good ones, suggesting that AI assistance served as a springboard for some juniors and a cushion for others."

So the split was among juniors, lawyers with fewer than seven years of experience (p. 23). Seniors gained: "Measured by unassisted judgment, only senior lawyers emerged from three months of AI use with improved capability" (p. 2). Fifteen of the 91 redlines showed possible AI use. Without them, the overall gain falls below conventional significance, while the senior gain holds at the 10 percent level (p. 3).

The authors are plain about the limit: "Our experiment does not answer why the effects appear positive for some lawyers and negative for others" (p. 2). It covers one profession, and the junior group was small. The tool was custom. The study was conducted by Google, Google funded its direct costs, and all eleven firms have patent-drafting relationships with Google.

The figure's two associates show one way the split among juniors could arise. The study's tested results are scores. Its look at reasons, "post-experiment interviews with treated participants and an LLM-based qualitative analysis of redlining submissions" (p. 29), is in supplementary materials "not intended for publication" (p. 9, note 8). The authors float time spent as one possible mechanism: "Juniors using AI worked faster but showed no unassisted gains" (p. 30). The figure's account, writing down what's new before drafting and reworking the call from it when a fact changes, is an illustration, not a finding.

Source: Autor, Rodchenko, Martin, Iscenko, Strand, Pearl & Ferere, "Does AI Assistance Enhance or Erode Expertise? Evidence from a Three-Month Field Experiment in Patent Drafting," NBER Working Paper 35720 (revised October 2026). Quotes are from the abstract unless a page is given. The associates, the invention, the claims, the older patent and the check are constructed.
